name: Floating Promise: Async Result Neither Awaited Nor Handled
description: An async function is called or a promise is created, and its result is discarded with no await, then, catch or return, so failures are lost and completion is not ordered.
extended_description: A promise that nobody observes can reject without any handler, which hides errors or crashes Node with an unhandled rejection. The calling code also carries on before the operation completes, so later steps may run against data that has not been written yet.
detection_methods: Look for calls to async functions or promise-returning APIs used as statements
Check that every promise is awaited, returned, combined or given a catch handler
potential_mitigations: Await the promise or return it to the caller
Attach a catch handler when fire-and-forget is intended
Enable a lint rule that rejects floating promises
mapping_rationale: Written for BETSY to cover a common function-level defect; not derived from an external catalog entry.

name: Async Callback Passed to an Iterator That Does Not Await It
description: An async function is given to forEach, or to map without collecting the resulting promises, so the loop finishes before any of the work does and failures are not caught.
extended_description: Array.prototype.forEach ignores the return value of its callback, so the promises an async callback returns are dropped. The surrounding function continues as if the work were done, errors become unhandled rejections, and code that relies on the results sees partial state. map with an async callback returns promises that still need awaiting.
detection_methods: Look for .forEach(async ...) and for array methods given async callbacks
Check that map with an async callback is wrapped in Promise.all
potential_mitigations: Use for...of with await for sequential work
Use await Promise.all(items.map(async ...)) for parallel work
mapping_rationale: Written for BETSY to cover a common function-level defect; not derived from an external catalog entry.

name: Numeric Parse Result Used Without a NaN Check
description: Text is converted to a number with parseInt, parseFloat, Number or unary plus and the result is used without testing whether the conversion failed.
extended_description: JavaScript's numeric conversions do not throw on bad input; they return NaN, or a partial value when parseInt stops at the first invalid character. NaN then spreads silently through arithmetic and makes every comparison false, so range checks pass or fail in surprising ways. parseInt without a radix also misreads some inputs.
detection_methods: Look for parseInt, parseFloat, Number() or unary plus on input text
Check for Number.isNaN, Number.isFinite or Number.isInteger before the value is used
potential_mitigations: Validate the result with Number.isFinite or Number.isInteger
Pass a radix to parseInt, or validate the whole string with a pattern first
mapping_rationale: Written for BETSY to cover a common function-level defect; not derived from an external catalog entry.

name: for...in Used to Iterate an Array or Untrusted Object
description: A for...in loop is used over an array, or over an object whose prototype chain may hold extra enumerable properties, so the loop sees unexpected keys or string indices.
extended_description: for...in enumerates enumerable string keys, including inherited ones. On arrays it yields indices as strings, can visit them out of order and includes any extra properties. On plain objects it also walks properties added to Object.prototype by libraries or by prototype pollution.
detection_methods: Look for for (const k in arr) where arr is an array
Look for for...in over objects with no hasOwnProperty check
potential_mitigations: Use for...of, forEach or an index loop for arrays
Use Object.keys, Object.entries or an Object.hasOwn check for objects
mapping_rationale: Written for BETSY to cover a common function-level defect; not derived from an external catalog entry.

name: typeof Object Test That Lets null Through
description: Code uses typeof x === 'object' to decide that a value is an object and then reads its properties, but typeof null is also 'object'.
extended_description: A historical quirk of JavaScript makes typeof null return 'object'. Guards that rely only on that test let null pass and then fail with a TypeError when a property is accessed. Arrays also pass the test, which may not be intended.
detection_methods: Look for typeof x === 'object' guards with no x !== null check
Check what happens next when the value is null or an array
potential_mitigations: Test x !== null alongside the typeof check
Use Array.isArray or a schema validator when the shape matters
mapping_rationale: Written for BETSY to cover a common function-level defect; not derived from an external catalog entry.

name: Assignment to an Undeclared Variable Creating an Implicit Global
description: A variable is assigned without let, const or var, so in non-strict JavaScript it silently becomes a property of the global object shared by all code.
extended_description: Outside strict mode, assigning to a name that has not been declared creates a global variable. Concurrent requests, other modules and later calls then share and overwrite it, causing state to leak between users or calls. A typo in a variable name produces the same effect.
detection_methods: Look for assignments to names that are never declared in scope
Check whether the file or function is in strict mode
potential_mitigations: Declare variables with let or const
Enable strict mode or use ES modules, which are strict by default
mapping_rationale: Written for BETSY to cover a common function-level defect; not derived from an external catalog entry.

name: Array Sorted Without a Comparator on Non-String Values
description: Array.prototype.sort or toSorted is called with no comparison function on numbers, dates or mixed values, so elements are compared as strings.
extended_description: Without a comparator JavaScript converts each element to a string and orders by UTF-16 code units. Numbers therefore sort as 1, 10, 2, and dates or objects sort by their string form. The result looks plausible on small test data and fails on real values.
detection_methods: Look for .sort() or .toSorted() with no argument
Check the element type of the array being sorted
potential_mitigations: Pass a comparator such as (a, b) => a - b
Use localeCompare for strings that need locale order
mapping_rationale: Written for BETSY to cover a common function-level defect; not derived from an external catalog entry.

name: Line Break After return Triggering Automatic Semicolon Insertion
description: A return statement is followed by a line break before its value, so JavaScript inserts a semicolon and the function returns undefined.
extended_description: JavaScript's grammar ends a return statement at a line break. When the returned object literal, array or expression starts on the next line, the function returns undefined and the following code is unreachable, without any error at run time.
detection_methods: Look for return on its own line followed by an expression on the next line
potential_mitigations: Start the returned expression on the same line as return, or wrap it in parentheses that open on that line
mapping_rationale: Written for BETSY to cover a common function-level defect; not derived from an external catalog entry.

name: Type Assertion Overriding the Type Checker
description: A TypeScript value is forced to another type with as any, a double assertion through unknown, or angle-bracket casts, hiding a real type mismatch from the compiler.
extended_description: Type assertions change only what the compiler believes, not the value at run time. Casting through any or unknown removes the check that the two types overlap, so a wrong shape reaches code that trusts it, and later property access or method calls fail or read undefined.
detection_methods: Look for as any, as unknown as T, <any> and similar casts
Check whether the asserted type matches what the value actually is
potential_mitigations: Fix the types, narrow with type guards, or validate at run time
Ban as any with a lint rule outside reviewed boundaries
mapping_rationale: Written for BETSY to cover a common function-level defect; not derived from an external catalog entry.

name: Non-Null Assertion on a Value That May Be Null or Undefined
description: The TypeScript ! postfix operator tells the compiler a value is present when the code has not shown that it is.
extended_description: The non-null assertion removes null and undefined from a type without any runtime check. Lookups such as Map.get, find, querySelector, optional fields and array indexing can all return nothing, and asserting otherwise moves the failure to a later TypeError or wrong result.
detection_methods: Look for the postfix ! operator on results of lookups, optional properties or DOM queries
potential_mitigations: Check for null or undefined and handle the missing case
Use optional chaining with a fallback where absence is acceptable
mapping_rationale: Written for BETSY to cover a common function-level defect; not derived from an external catalog entry.

name: Type Errors Suppressed With ts-ignore or ts-expect-error
description: A suppression comment tells the TypeScript compiler to skip a line or file, hiding a type error in code that is actually wrong.
extended_description: Suppression comments turn off type checking for the following line or file. They are sometimes used to get a build to pass when a value has the wrong type, an argument is missing or a property does not exist. The underlying defect then ships unchecked, and later type changes are hidden as well.
detection_methods: Search for @ts-ignore, @ts-expect-error and @ts-nocheck comments and inspect the suppressed line
potential_mitigations: Fix the type error, or replace the suppression with a narrow, documented type guard
mapping_rationale: Written for BETSY to cover a common function-level defect; not derived from an external catalog entry.

name: External Data Asserted to a Declared Type Without Runtime Validation
description: Parsed JSON, a response body, storage contents or message data is cast to a TypeScript type and trusted without checking that it has that shape.
extended_description: TypeScript types are erased at run time. Writing JSON.parse(text) as User or await res.json() as Order makes the compiler trust the shape, but nothing enforces it. Missing fields, wrong types or extra properties from a client, server or file then reach code that assumes they are valid.
detection_methods: Look for JSON.parse, response.json(), localStorage reads or message data cast with as or assigned to a typed variable
Check for a schema validator or type guard between parsing and use
potential_mitigations: Validate with a schema library such as zod, io-ts, valibot or ajv
Write a type guard that checks each required field
mapping_rationale: Written for BETSY to cover a common function-level defect; not derived from an external catalog entry.

name: Mutable Default Argument Shared Across Calls
description: A Python function uses a list, dict, set or other mutable object as a default parameter value and then changes it, so the change persists into later calls.
extended_description: Default values in Python are evaluated once, when the function is defined. A mutable default is therefore one object shared by every call that omits the argument. Appending to it or setting keys accumulates state across calls and across users, a frequent source of surprising bugs.
detection_methods: Look for def f(x=[]), x={}, x=set() or a default that constructs a mutable object
Check whether the function mutates that parameter
potential_mitigations: Default to None and create a new object inside the function
mapping_rationale: Written for BETSY to cover a common function-level defect; not derived from an external catalog entry.

name: Closure Capturing a Loop Variable by Late Binding
description: Functions created inside a loop refer to the loop variable itself rather than its value at that iteration, so when called later they all see its final value.
extended_description: Python closures and JavaScript functions over var bind names, not values. A lambda, callback or nested function defined in a loop and run after the loop finishes sees whatever the variable held last. Every handler then acts on the same item.
detection_methods: Look for lambdas or nested functions created in loops that use the loop variable
In JavaScript, check whether the loop variable is declared with var
potential_mitigations: In Python, bind the value with a default argument or functools.partial
In JavaScript, declare the loop variable with let or const
mapping_rationale: Written for BETSY to cover a common function-level defect; not derived from an external catalog entry.

name: Collection Modified While Being Iterated
description: A list, dict, set, array or map is changed by adding or removing elements during a loop over that same collection.
extended_description: Changing a collection's size while iterating over it either raises an error, as with Python dicts and sets, or silently skips or repeats elements, as with Python lists and JavaScript arrays. The bug is often invisible on test data where nothing gets removed.
detection_methods: Look for remove, pop, del, append, splice or delete on the collection being iterated
Check removal patterns inside forEach and for...of loops
potential_mitigations: Iterate over a copy, or build a new collection with the kept items
Collect changes and apply them after the loop
Iterate backwards by index when removing in place
mapping_rationale: Written for BETSY to cover a common function-level defect; not derived from an external catalog entry.

name: assert Used for Runtime Validation That Optimisation Removes
description: Input checks, permission checks or other conditions the program depends on are written as assert statements, which are removed when Python runs with -O or C is built with NDEBUG.
extended_description: Assertions document assumptions and are meant to be disabled in optimised builds. When an assert is the only thing rejecting bad input, an unauthorised caller or a missing value, that protection disappears in production configurations, and the code proceeds with the invalid state.
detection_methods: Look for assert statements that test parameters, input data, permissions or return values from calls that can fail
potential_mitigations: Replace with explicit checks that raise an exception or return an error
mapping_rationale: Written for BETSY to cover a common function-level defect; not derived from an external catalog entry.

name: Truthiness Test Where a Missing-Value Check Was Intended
description: Code checks if not x, if (!x) or x || default to detect a missing value, but valid values such as 0, an empty string, an empty list or false also fail the test.
extended_description: Python and JavaScript treat several legitimate values as false. A guard meant to catch None, null or undefined therefore also rejects a zero quantity, an empty name or a false flag, or replaces them with a default. The bug shows up only for those edge values.
detection_methods: Look for if not x or if (!x) on optional parameters that can legitimately be 0, empty or false
Look for x or default and x || default on such values
potential_mitigations: Test x is None in Python
Use x == null, x === undefined or the ?? operator in JavaScript
mapping_rationale: Written for BETSY to cover a common function-level defect; not derived from an external catalog entry.

name: One-Shot Iterator or Generator Consumed More Than Once
description: A generator, map or filter object, file iterator or other single-pass iterator is looped over twice, and the second pass silently sees no items.
extended_description: Many Python and JavaScript iteration objects can be traversed only once. After the first loop, sum, list conversion or membership test exhausts them, later passes yield nothing without raising an error, so counts become zero and checks quietly fail.
detection_methods: Look for generators, map, filter, zip or file objects stored in a variable and iterated more than once
Check for in tests on iterators, which consume them
potential_mitigations: Convert to a list or tuple once before reuse
Recreate the iterator for each pass
mapping_rationale: Written for BETSY to cover a common function-level defect; not derived from an external catalog entry.

name: Naive and Time-Zone-Aware Date-Times Mixed
description: Date-time values with and without a time zone, or values in local time and UTC, are compared, subtracted or stored together as if they were the same kind.
extended_description: A naive date-time carries no zone, so its meaning depends on the machine running the code. Mixing naive and aware values raises errors in Python, and treating local time as UTC, or parsing date-only strings as UTC in JavaScript, shifts results by hours and breaks around daylight-saving changes.
detection_methods: Look for datetime.now(), utcnow() or fromtimestamp() without tz compared with aware values
Look for new Date(string) on date-only or zone-less strings and getHours rather than getUTCHours
potential_mitigations: Use aware date-times in UTC internally, such as datetime.now(timezone.utc)
Parse with an explicit zone and convert to local time only for display
mapping_rationale: Written for BETSY to cover a common function-level defect; not derived from an external catalog entry.

name: Exception Escaping a Destructor or noexcept Function
description: A C++ destructor, or a function declared noexcept, can let an exception propagate, which calls std::terminate and stops the program.
extended_description: Destructors are implicitly noexcept, and functions marked noexcept promise not to throw. If an exception leaves either, the runtime calls std::terminate without unwinding further. Destructors that close files, flush buffers or call other code that can throw are the usual cause, as are move constructors marked noexcept.
detection_methods: Look for calls that can throw inside destructors and noexcept functions without a try/catch
Look for explicit throw statements in those functions
potential_mitigations: Catch and handle or log exceptions inside the destructor
Move fallible cleanup into an explicit close method that callers can check
mapping_rationale: Written for BETSY to cover a common function-level defect; not derived from an external catalog entry.

name: Iterator, Pointer or Reference Used After Container Mutation Invalidates It
description: An iterator, pointer or reference into a C++ container is kept across an operation that can reallocate or remove elements, and is then used.
extended_description: Operations such as push_back, insert, erase, resize and rehash can move or free a container's elements. Iterators, pointers and references obtained earlier then refer to freed or shifted memory. Erasing inside a range loop and pushing into a vector while holding a reference to one of its elements are common forms.
detection_methods: Look for push_back, insert, emplace, erase or resize while an iterator, pointer or reference into the same container is alive
Look for erase inside range-based for loops
potential_mitigations: Use the iterator returned by erase, or the erase-remove idiom
Reserve capacity first, or store indices instead of pointers
mapping_rationale: Written for BETSY to cover a common function-level defect; not derived from an external catalog entry.

name: View or Reference Bound to a Temporary That Outlives It
description: A std::string_view, std::span, const reference member, c_str() pointer or similar non-owning handle is taken from a temporary object and used after that temporary is destroyed.
extended_description: Temporaries live only until the end of the full expression that creates them, unless bound directly to a local reference. Taking a view, a raw pointer or a reference to a member of a temporary, or of a range in a range-based for, leaves the handle dangling as soon as the statement ends.
detection_methods: Look for string_view or span variables initialised from function results that return by value
Look for c_str() or data() of temporary strings stored in variables
Look for range-based for over a member of a temporary
potential_mitigations: Store the owning object in a named variable first
Return owning types instead of views from functions
mapping_rationale: Written for BETSY to cover a common function-level defect; not derived from an external catalog entry.

name: Object Used After Being Moved From
description: A C++ object is passed to std::move or otherwise moved from, and then read as if it still held its original value.
extended_description: After a move the source is in a valid but unspecified state; strings and containers are usually empty, smart pointers are null. Code that keeps reading the moved-from object sees empty or default values, or dereferences a null pointer.
detection_methods: Look for uses of a variable after it appears as std::move(x) or is passed to a by-value or rvalue-reference parameter
potential_mitigations: Do not use the variable after moving it, or reassign it first
Move only at the last use
mapping_rationale: Written for BETSY to cover a common function-level defect; not derived from an external catalog entry.

name: Mutex Locked and Unlocked by Hand Instead of With a Scoped Guard
description: A C++ mutex is locked with lock() and released with unlock(), so an early return, break or exception between them leaves it locked.
extended_description: Manual pairing of lock and unlock depends on every path reaching the unlock. Exceptions, early returns and later edits break that easily, leaving the mutex held and deadlocking the next thread that needs it. RAII guards release the lock automatically when the scope ends.
detection_methods: Look for mutex.lock() and mutex.unlock() calls in the same function
Check every path between them for returns, breaks and calls that can throw
potential_mitigations: Use std::lock_guard, std::unique_lock or std::scoped_lock
mapping_rationale: Written for BETSY to cover a common function-level defect; not derived from an external catalog entry.

name: Derived Object Sliced by Copying Into a Base Value
description: A derived class object is copied into a variable, parameter or container element of its base class type, losing its derived part and virtual behaviour.
extended_description: Copying by value to a base type keeps only the base subobject. Virtual calls on the copy then use the base implementation, and derived data is dropped. This happens with by-value parameters, catch by value, and containers such as std::vector<Base>.
detection_methods: Look for base-class parameters, locals or container element types holding derived objects by value
Look for catch clauses that take exceptions by value
potential_mitigations: Pass and store by reference or smart pointer
Catch exceptions by const reference
Make base classes non-copyable
mapping_rationale: Written for BETSY to cover a common function-level defect; not derived from an external catalog entry.

name: Virtual Function Called From a Constructor or Destructor
description: A C++ constructor or destructor calls a virtual member function, expecting the derived override, but the call resolves to the class being constructed or destroyed.
extended_description: During construction and destruction the dynamic type is the class whose constructor or destructor is running. Virtual calls made there do not reach derived overrides, and calling a pure virtual function at that point is undefined behaviour that usually aborts.
detection_methods: Look for calls to virtual members, directly or through helpers, inside constructors and destructors
potential_mitigations: Move the call into a separate init step after construction
Pass the needed data to the base constructor
mapping_rationale: Written for BETSY to cover a common function-level defect; not derived from an external catalog entry.

name: Lambda Capturing Locals by Reference That Outlives Their Scope
description: A C++ lambda captures local variables by reference with [&] or [&x] and is stored, returned, or handed to a thread or callback that runs after the function returns.
extended_description: Reference captures do not extend lifetimes. Once the enclosing function returns, the captured locals are destroyed and the lambda's references dangle. Asynchronous APIs such as std::thread, std::async, event loops and callback registrations make this easy to miss.
detection_methods: Look for [&] or [&x] lambdas passed to threads, async tasks, callbacks or stored in members
Check whether the lambda can run after the scope ends
potential_mitigations: Capture by value or move ownership into the lambda
Use shared_ptr for state the callback needs
mapping_rationale: Written for BETSY to cover a common function-level defect; not derived from an external catalog entry.

name: std::thread Destroyed While Joinable or Detached While Using Locals
description: A std::thread object goes out of scope without join or detach, which terminates the program, or is detached while still using data owned by the function.
extended_description: Destroying a joinable std::thread calls std::terminate. Early returns or exceptions between creating the thread and joining it trigger this. Detaching avoids the crash but leaves the thread running after the function returns, so any reference to the function's locals dangles.
detection_methods: Look for std::thread locals with paths that skip join
Look for detach on threads that use references or pointers to locals
potential_mitigations: Use std::jthread or an RAII joiner
Pass data to detached threads by value or shared ownership
mapping_rationale: Written for BETSY to cover a common function-level defect; not derived from an external catalog entry.

name: Lock Guard or RefCell Borrow Held Across an await or Re-entrant Call
description: Rust code keeps a MutexGuard, RwLock guard or RefCell borrow alive across an await point or a call that may lock or borrow the same value again.
extended_description: A guard held across await can deadlock when another task on the same executor needs the lock, and std guards also make the future non-Send. A RefCell borrow held while calling code that borrows the same cell mutably panics at run time with a BorrowMutError.
detection_methods: Look for guards or borrows bound with let and still in scope at an .await
Look for callbacks or methods called while a RefCell borrow is held
potential_mitigations: Limit guard scope with a block or drop before await
Use an async-aware mutex where holding across await is needed
Clone the needed data out before calling back
mapping_rationale: Written for BETSY to cover a common function-level defect; not derived from an external catalog entry.

name: Structure With Uninitialised Padding Copied Across a Trust Boundary
description: A structure is filled member by member and then written whole to another process, the kernel's caller, a file or the network, so the padding bytes between members carry stale memory with it.
extended_description: Compilers insert padding to align members, and setting each member leaves those bytes holding whatever was on the stack or heap before. Copying sizeof the structure to user space, a socket or a file therefore discloses old data such as pointers or keys.
detection_methods: Find structures sent with copy_to_user, send, write, fwrite or memcpy into an output buffer using sizeof the structure
Check whether the structure was zeroed as a whole before its members were set
potential_mitigations: Clear the whole structure with memset or = {0} before setting members
Serialise member by member, or declare the type packed when the layout allows it

name: Function Attributed Unsequenced or Reproducible but Having Side Effects
description: A C23 function carries the unsequenced or reproducible attribute, which lets the compiler merge or reorder its calls, yet its body changes or depends on state the attribute rules out.
extended_description: These attributes promise that calls with equal arguments can be combined or reordered. A body that writes a global, performs I/O, reads volatile objects or, for unsequenced, reads mutable globals breaks that promise, and optimised code may skip or reorder the calls.
detection_methods: Find functions declared with [[unsequenced]] or [[reproducible]]
Check their bodies for writes to globals or statics, I/O, volatile access or calls to functions with effects
potential_mitigations: Remove the attribute
Move the side effects out of the attributed function

name: Objects Compared Byte-Wise Including Padding or Non-Value Bits
description: Two structures, floating-point values or class objects are compared with memcmp or an equivalent raw byte comparison, so padding bytes, alternate encodings and hidden members decide the result instead of the values.
extended_description: Padding has unspecified contents, so equal members can compare unequal. Floating-point zero has two encodings and NaN is never equal to itself, yet byte comparison says otherwise. Polymorphic C++ objects contain a hidden virtual table pointer, and classes such as std::string hold pointers to their data.
detection_methods: Find memcmp, bcmp or byte-loop comparisons whose operands are structs, unions, floating-point values or class objects
Check whether the type has padding, floating-point members or non-trivial members
potential_mitigations: Compare member by member
Define operator== or a comparison function that compares values

name: Modification of a String Returned by getenv, setlocale, localeconv or strerror
description: Code writes through a pointer returned by a library function that owns the storage and does not allow callers to change it, such as getenv, setlocale, localeconv, strerror or asctime.
extended_description: The standard library may return a pointer into static or environment storage. Writing to it is undefined, can corrupt the environment of the process, and can change what later callers of the same function see.
detection_methods: Find writes, strcat, strtok or in-place transforms applied to the result of getenv, setlocale, localeconv, strerror or asctime
Check whether the result was copied first
potential_mitigations: Copy the result into a buffer the function owns before changing it
Treat the result as pointer to const

name: Pointer From getenv, strerror or envp Used After a Later Call Invalidates It
description: A pointer returned by getenv, strerror, setlocale or localeconv, or taken from the envp array, is kept and read after a later call that may overwrite or reallocate the storage it points to.
extended_description: Several library functions reuse one static buffer, so the second call changes what the first pointer shows. Changing the environment with setenv or putenv can reallocate the array that envp points to, leaving the old pointer dangling.
detection_methods: Track pointers from getenv, strerror, setlocale, localeconv and envp across later calls to the same family or to setenv, putenv and unsetenv
Check whether the first result was copied before those calls
potential_mitigations: Copy the result before calling the function again
Read the environment through environ after changing it, not through envp

name: Exit Handler That Calls exit or longjmp Instead of Returning
description: A function registered with atexit or at_quick_exit ends the program again or jumps away with longjmp rather than returning, which is undefined and can skip the remaining handlers.
extended_description: Handlers run during program termination. Calling exit from inside one re-enters termination, and longjmp out of one leaves the process in an undefined state. Other registered handlers and stream flushing may never run.
detection_methods: Find functions passed to atexit or at_quick_exit, or C++ functions registered for termination
Check whether they call exit, quick_exit or longjmp, directly or through helpers in the same body
potential_mitigations: Return normally from every exit handler
Use _Exit only when skipping remaining cleanup is intended

name: Signal Handler for SIGFPE, SIGSEGV or SIGILL That Returns
description: A handler for a computational exception signal returns normally, so execution resumes at the faulting instruction with undefined results.
extended_description: After an arithmetic fault, invalid access or illegal instruction the program cannot safely continue at the point of failure. Returning from the handler usually repeats the fault forever or continues with corrupted state.
detection_methods: Find handlers installed with signal or sigaction for SIGFPE, SIGSEGV, SIGILL or SIGBUS
Check whether every path ends in _Exit, abort or siglongjmp
potential_mitigations: End the handler with _Exit or abort
Prevent the fault with checks instead of catching it

name: errno Read Without Being Reset or Without a Failure Indicator
description: Code tests errno to decide whether a library call failed, but either did not set errno to zero before the call or reads it even though the call's return value did not report failure.
extended_description: Successful calls may leave errno unchanged or set it to an unrelated value, so a non-zero errno alone says nothing about the last call. Functions such as strtol report range errors only through errno, which must be cleared beforehand.
detection_methods: Find conditions on errno after library calls
Check for errno = 0 before calls that need it and for a test of the return value before relying on errno
potential_mitigations: Set errno to zero before strtol, strtod and similar calls
Check the return value first and read errno only when it signals failure

name: Stream Switched Between Reading and Writing Without a Flush or Seek
description: A file opened for update is read and then written, or written and then read, with no flush or positioning call between the two, which the C library leaves undefined.
extended_description: Update streams share one buffer for input and output. Switching direction without fflush, fseek, fsetpos or rewind may lose data, write at the wrong place or return stale bytes. C++ file streams behave the same way.
detection_methods: Find FILE streams opened with + modes, or fstream objects used for both reading and writing
Check that a flush or seek separates each change of direction
potential_mitigations: Call fflush after output and fseek or rewind before switching to input, and seek before switching to output
Use separate streams or reopen the file

name: Mutex Destroyed While Still Locked or in Use
description: A mutex is destroyed, or the object owning it is destroyed, while the mutex is locked or while other threads may still lock it.
extended_description: Destroying a held mutex is undefined in C threads, POSIX and C++. A common form is a mutex that is local to a function which starts threads using it and returns before joining them.
detection_methods: Find pthread_mutex_destroy, mtx_destroy or the end of scope of a std::mutex
Check that the mutex is unlocked and all threads using it have finished first
potential_mitigations: Unlock and join all users before destroying the mutex
Give the mutex a lifetime longer than every thread that uses it

name: Condition Wait or Weak Compare-Exchange Not Retried in a Loop
description: A thread waits on a condition variable once, guarded by an if rather than a loop over the predicate, or calls a weak compare-exchange once, so spurious wake-ups and spurious failures are taken as real outcomes.
extended_description: Condition waits may return without a notification, and another thread may change the state between the notify and the wake-up. Weak compare-exchange may fail even when the values match. Each must be retried until the condition truly holds.
detection_methods: Find condition waits and check that they sit inside a while loop over the predicate or use a predicate overload
Find compare_exchange_weak calls and check that they are retried in a loop
potential_mitigations: Wrap the wait in while (!predicate)
Use the predicate overload of wait, or loop around weak compare-exchange

name: Condition Variable Notified or Waited Inconsistently
description: A condition variable shared by waiters with different predicates is signalled with a single-waiter notify, or the same condition variable is waited on with different mutexes, so threads miss wake-ups or behave undefinedly.
extended_description: A single notify wakes an arbitrary waiter, which may not be the one whose condition became true; it goes back to sleep and the right one never wakes. POSIX leaves waiting on one condition variable with two different mutexes undefined.
detection_methods: Find notify_one, pthread_cond_signal or cnd_signal on condition variables waited on for different conditions
Find one condition variable waited on with different mutexes
potential_mitigations: Use notify_all or broadcast when waiters test different predicates
Use one condition variable per predicate and always the same mutex

name: Thread Terminated by a Signal or by Asynchronous Cancellation
description: A thread is stopped from outside with pthread_kill and a terminating signal or with asynchronous cancellation, so it can be cut off while holding locks or with data half updated.
extended_description: Asynchronous cancellation can take effect at any instruction, including inside malloc or while a mutex is held. Sending SIGKILL or SIGTERM to one thread ends the whole process. Neither lets the thread release resources in order.
detection_methods: Find pthread_kill with terminating signals
Find pthread_setcanceltype with PTHREAD_CANCEL_ASYNCHRONOUS
potential_mitigations: Use a shared stop flag that the thread checks
Use deferred cancellation with cleanup handlers

name: Declaration Parsed as a Function or an Unnamed Temporary Instead of an Object
description: A C++ statement meant to create an object is parsed as a function declaration or creates a temporary that is destroyed at once, so a lock, timer or guard does nothing.
extended_description: Empty parentheses after a variable name declare a function. Writing a type with a constructor argument but no variable name, such as std::lock_guard<std::mutex>(m);, either declares a variable named m or makes a temporary that ends at the semicolon, so the critical section is unprotected.
detection_methods: Find guard or RAII types constructed without a variable name
Find declarations like T x(); intended to create an object
potential_mitigations: Name every guard object
Use brace initialisation or class template argument deduction with a name
common_consequences: Code Does Not Run as Written

name: Array of Derived Objects Indexed or Deleted Through a Base Pointer
description: An array of derived class objects is accessed with pointer arithmetic or deleted through a pointer to the base class, so the element size used is wrong.
extended_description: Indexing uses the size of the static type, so p[1] on a Base pointer to Derived objects lands inside the first object when the sizes differ. delete[] through a base pointer is undefined even with a virtual destructor.
detection_methods: Find new Derived[n] assigned to a Base pointer
Find functions taking Base* and indexing it when callers pass derived arrays
potential_mitigations: Store pointers or smart pointers to the objects in a container
Keep the array typed as the derived class

name: Iterator Range Built From Different Containers or With Reversed Bounds
description: An algorithm or container member is given a begin iterator and an end iterator that come from different containers, or a first iterator that lies after the last, so it walks off the intended range.
extended_description: Standard algorithms assume last is reachable from first by incrementing. Mixing iterators of two containers, or passing them in the wrong order, makes the algorithm read or write unrelated memory.
detection_methods: Find algorithm calls whose iterator arguments name different containers
Find ranges built from computed iterators that may be out of order
potential_mitigations: Pass begin and end of the same container, or use ranges algorithms that take the container
Check that computed positions are ordered before forming a range

name: Stateful Predicate Passed to an Algorithm That May Copy It
description: A function object or mutable lambda that changes its own state on each call is passed to a standard algorithm, which may copy the predicate and call different copies.
extended_description: Algorithms such as remove_if take predicates by value and may copy them internally, so state like a call counter is split across copies. A predicate that removes, for example, the third element can remove others as well.
detection_methods: Find predicates with mutable captures or data members changed in operator()
Check whether they are passed to remove_if, find_if, partition or similar
potential_mitigations: Make predicates stateless
Keep state outside and capture it by reference, or wrap the predicate in std::ref

name: Object Used in Raw Storage Without Construction or Destruction
description: Memory from malloc, a char buffer or an allocator is used as an object of a class type without constructing it, or the memory is released without running the object's destructor.
extended_description: Only trivial types may be used in storage without construction. Classes with constructors, virtual functions or owning members need placement new or std::construct_at, and an explicit destructor call before the storage is freed or reused.
detection_methods: Find malloc, calloc, realloc or allocator allocate results cast to class types and used
Find free or deallocate of storage holding non-trivial objects without a destructor call
potential_mitigations: Construct with placement new or std::construct_at and destroy with std::destroy_at
Use new and delete, or containers, instead of raw storage

name: Object Constructed in Misaligned or Undersized Storage
description: Placement new or std::construct_at builds an object in a buffer that is smaller than the type or not aligned for it, or an over-aligned type is allocated with a plain allocator that ignores its alignment.
extended_description: A char array has alignment one, so constructing a double or a class with stricter alignment inside it is undefined. A buffer shorter than sizeof the type is overrun by the constructor. Before C++17, new of an over-aligned type did not honour the alignment.
detection_methods: Find placement new into char or byte arrays and check their size and alignas
Find types declared with large alignas allocated through plain operator new or malloc
potential_mitigations: Declare buffers with alignas(T) and at least sizeof(T) bytes
Use aligned allocation functions for over-aligned types

name: Replacement Allocator or Handler Violating Its Standard Contract
description: A user-supplied operator new, new handler or terminate handler behaves in a way the standard forbids, such as returning a null pointer from a throwing operator new or returning from a terminate handler.
extended_description: Code that calls new assumes it either returns usable memory or throws std::bad_alloc. A replacement that returns nullptr leads callers to dereference null. A terminate handler must end the program, and a new handler must free memory, throw or end the program.
detection_methods: Find definitions of operator new, operator delete, set_new_handler or set_terminate callbacks
Check what each does on failure
potential_mitigations: Throw std::bad_alloc on allocation failure in throwing forms
Make terminate handlers call std::abort

name: Constructor or Destructor Function-Try-Block Handler Using Members
description: The catch clause of a function-try-block on a constructor or destructor reads or calls members or base classes, which have already been destroyed or were never constructed when the handler runs.
extended_description: If a member initialiser or the body throws, all constructed members and bases are destroyed before control reaches the handler. Referring to them there is undefined.
detection_methods: Find constructors and destructors written as try : init { } catch (...) { }
Check whether the handler uses this, members or bases
potential_mitigations: Only log, translate or rethrow in such handlers
Move cleanup into members' own destructors

name: Broad Exception Handler Placed Before a More Specific One
description: In one try statement a handler for a base exception class comes before a handler for one of its subclasses, so the specific handler can never run.
extended_description: Handlers are tried in order and the first match wins. Catching std::exception before std::runtime_error, or Exception before ValueError, makes the later clause dead code and applies generic handling where special handling was intended.
detection_methods: List the handlers of each try in order
Check whether an earlier handler's type is a base of a later one
potential_mitigations: Order handlers from most derived to most general

name: Exception Caught by Value or Thrown and Caught by Pointer
description: A C++ handler catches a class-type exception by value, which slices derived exceptions and copies them, or the code throws pointers to heap exceptions that handlers must remember to delete.
extended_description: Catching by value copies only the base part of a derived exception, losing its type and data, and the copy can itself throw. Throwing new E leaks the exception object unless every handler deletes it.
detection_methods: Find catch clauses whose parameter is a class type without &
Find throw new and catch of pointer types
potential_mitigations: Throw by value and catch by const reference

name: Derived Object Deleted Through a Base Class Without a Virtual Destructor
description: A derived object created with new is deleted, or owned by a smart pointer, through a pointer to a base class whose destructor is not virtual, so the derived destructor does not run.
extended_description: Deleting through a base pointer is undefined unless the base destructor is virtual. In practice the derived part is not destroyed, which leaks its resources. std::unique_ptr<Base> holding a Derived has the same problem.
detection_methods: Find new Derived stored in a Base pointer or unique_ptr<Base> and later deleted
Check whether Base declares a virtual destructor where visible
potential_mitigations: Declare the base destructor virtual
Keep ownership in the derived type, or use std::shared_ptr created from the derived type

name: Constructor Initialiser Reads a Member Not Yet Initialised
description: A member initialiser list uses another member's value, but that member is declared later in the class and so is initialised later, whatever order the list is written in.
extended_description: Members are initialised in declaration order. An initialiser such as len(buf.size()) runs before buf is constructed if len is declared first, so it reads an indeterminate value.
detection_methods: For each mem-initialiser that reads another member, compare declaration order where the class is visible
Watch for initialiser lists written in a different order from the declarations
potential_mitigations: Initialise from constructor parameters instead of other members
Reorder member declarations to match dependencies

name: Copy Assignment That Breaks on Self-Assignment
description: A copy assignment operator releases the object's current resources and then copies from the source, so assigning an object to itself reads data it has just freed.
extended_description: With a = a, the source and target are the same object. Deleting the target's buffer first leaves the source pointer dangling, and the following copy reads freed memory.
detection_methods: Find user-defined operator= that delete or free members before copying from the argument
Check for a self-assignment test or copy-and-swap
potential_mitigations: Use copy-and-swap
Copy into a new buffer before releasing the old one, or test this != &other

name: Pointer-to-Member Applied to an Object That Lacks That Member
description: A pointer to a member of a derived class is converted to a pointer to member of the base and applied with .* or ->* to an object whose dynamic type does not have the member.
extended_description: Converting member pointers up the hierarchy is allowed with a cast, but using one on an object that is only the base type reaches memory or a function that does not exist for that object.
detection_methods: Find static_cast between pointer-to-member types
Check the dynamic type of objects they are applied to
potential_mitigations: Apply member pointers only to objects of the class that declares the member
Use virtual functions instead of member pointer casts

name: Copy Operation That Modifies Its Source Object
description: A copy constructor or copy assignment operator changes the object it copies from, so copies made by containers and algorithms silently alter the originals.
extended_description: Standard containers and algorithms copy values freely and assume the source is unchanged. Moving ownership out of the source in a copy operation, like the old auto_ptr, leaves originals empty after a sort or a push_back.
detection_methods: Find copy constructors and assignment operators
Check for writes to the source, mutable members changed, or const_cast on it
potential_mitigations: Leave the source unchanged in copy operations
Implement transfer of ownership as a move operation instead

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Copy operations must not mutate the source object

name: Function Declared noreturn That Can Return
description: A function declared [[noreturn]] or _Noreturn has a path on which it returns to its caller, which is undefined because callers are compiled assuming it never does.
extended_description: The compiler may drop the code after a call to a noreturn function, so returning from it falls into whatever follows. Typical causes are a conditional exit or a loop that can end.
detection_methods: Find functions declared [[noreturn]] or _Noreturn
Check that every path calls another noreturn function, throws or loops forever
potential_mitigations: End every path with abort, exit, a throw or an infinite loop
Remove the attribute if the function can return
common_consequences: Execution Continues Past an Expected Exit
